procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of detention under s. 3 and the direction under the proviso to s. 8 of the Act passed by the District Magistrate on 9th May.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Petition under Art. 32 of the Constitution of India for a writ in the nature of habeas corpus.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner's signatures were taken on a blank sheet of paper without being informed of the contents.

facts: The petitioner claimed that his signatures were taken on a blank sheet of paper and that he was not informed of the contents.
An endorsement was made in Urdu on the back of the paper, stating that the petitioner had been informed as directed.
The petitioner's signature was placed under this Urdu endorsement.
The petitioner's signature was also in Urdu, and his handwriting indicated that he could read and write Urdu very well.
application: The court found the petitioner's claim that he signed a blank paper to be "totally false."
The court reasoned that since the petitioner signed in Urdu, a language he clearly understood, directly under an endorsement also written in Urdu, he must have known what he was signing.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, concluding that he must have been aware of the contents of the document he signed.

issue.issue_text: Whether it was necessary to serve a copy of the direction on the petitioner, under which he was informed that it was not in the public interest to disclose the grounds for his detention.

facts: The petitioner was detained and informed that it was against the public interest to disclose the grounds for his detention.
The petitioner argued that he should have been served with a physical copy of the written direction that authorized this non-disclosure.
The petitioner's counsel cited the case of Harikishan v. The State of Maharashtra to support this argument.
law: The precedent set in Harikishan v. The State of Maharashtra required that a copy of the grounds of detention be delivered to the detenu.
The proviso to section 8 of the relevant Act allows the authorities to decide not to disclose the grounds of detention if it is against the public interest.
application: The Court distinguished the current case from the Harikishan case.

It reasoned that the Harikishan case applied when the grounds of detention were actually being communicated; the purpose of serving a copy in that instance was to allow the detenu to know the grounds in detail in order to make a representation.
In the present case, under the proviso to section 8, no grounds were served at all. The petitioner was only to be informed of the decision not to disclose them.

The Court determined that for such a simple piece of information (that grounds would not be disclosed), there was no need to serve a physical copy of the order on the petitioner, as the rationale for doing so in the Harikishan case (enabling a representation against the grounds) did not apply.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that it was not necessary to serve him with a copy of the direction. Simply informing him that the grounds for his detention would not be disclosed in the public interest was sufficient.

issue.issue_text: Whether the use of the expression 'has been detained' in the order, implying the petitioner was already under detention when the order was made, rendered the detention illegal.

facts: On May 9th, 1970, the District Magistrate issued an order for the petitioner's detention.
On the same day, the District Magistrate issued a related direction which referred to the petitioner as a person who 'has been detained'.
Affidavits filed by the government established that the petitioner was actually taken into custody on May 22nd, 1970, not before the order was issued.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged that the language used in the direction was 'incorrect'.
The Court determined that the District Magistrate had simply made a 'mistake' by using the past tense expression 'has been'.
The Court noted that the detention order and the direction were passed on the same day, and the actual detention occurred later, as proven by affidavits.
The Court reasoned that this grammatical error or 'incorrect expression' did not change the factual reality of when the detention took place.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that the mistaken use of the phrase 'has been detained' in the order did not render the detention illegal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A detention order is not rendered illegal due to minor linguistic deviations from the authorizing statute, such as using the phrase "acting in 'a' manner" instead of "acting in 'any' manner." Furthermore, withholding the grounds for detention for reasons of "security of the State" is permissible under a statute that allows non-disclosure in the "public interest," as the former is inherently included within the latter.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The petitioner's detention is valid because the various challenges raised against the detention order are without merit. The factual claim regarding the signature was found to be false upon review of the original document, and the other arguments concerning the wording of the order and the service of a direction were dismissed as legally insignificant procedural or grammatical points that do not invalidate the detention.
legal_tests_applied: Any action in the interest of the security of the State is clearly in public interest.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioner's factual assertion that his signatures were taken on a blank paper was determined to be 'totally false' after the court examined the original order.

The court ruled that when the petitioner was informed that it was not in the public interest to disclose the grounds for his detention, there was 'no need to serve on him the copy of the direction under which he was so informed.'

The argument that the use of the phrase 'has been detained' invalidated the order was rejected, with the court finding that the 'use of this incorrect expression does not implv that the detention was illegal.'
why_respondent_won: The government's position was validated by the court's direct examination of the original order, which contradicted the petitioner's factual claims about signing a blank paper.
The court affirmed that the legal requirement was to inform the petitioner of the non-disclosure, not to formally serve him with the written direction authorizing it.
The court accepted that a grammatical error or an 'incorrect expression' in the wording of the detention order does not affect the substantive legality of the detention itself.
